title: Love's own jobs: Lyric Theater, Robichaux, Lee Collins and Kid Punch
summary: In one long account Love covers 1917 Chicago, returning to New Orleans, the Lyric Theater job with Robichaux, Cabaret work, replacement by Lee Collins, and working with Big Eye Louis.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: No, I don't think it was that far back. That's it. Dewey used to wait on Basin Street, Emmanuel Perez. That's when I was very small. Yeah, that must bring back. Let's see, wait, I got to get that thing straight. I think Tom could tell you better than I could about that. Tom Alba? Yeah. Because I had learned how to play cornet, you know, and Tom was playing the violin. And Eddie Vincent was practicing every day with us. And then all at once he picked up and he left there with Jimmy Fallon and then we went north. Well, he learned a lot when he was gone, you know. Went all over the Pantages time, I think they call it. All around and they come back, you see. Stomped in Chicago. Well, I was gone. I had been there and left. That was about around, well, I don't want to say because I don't know exactly. But it must have been 19, it was 1917. Because I remember Freddie Kepard come in and him and I played together, you know, on a show one night. We were giving a term for a sick musician in the roadhouse. We played together and I didn't get to see Louie or none of them. I flew around and I left Chicago and come back to Shreveport. Later after that, got Louie come in. Freddie stayed. And that left Louie, yeah, he got him another job around here, working around, you know, a different band. And when I left Shreveport, I come back to New Orleans. And Andrew Kimball was playing the cornet at the Lyric Theater with John Robichaud. And John told me Kimball was going to leave, you know. And said, the theater's closed now. I said, Kimball gonna leave. And I would have the job. And said, you about the fella for this job. You been playing shows. I said, well, I'd like to get you to play with me in the theater when it opens. I said, well, when it's gonna open? And he said, well, I don't know exactly, but three or four weeks after the repair up and everything, I said, I got Big Eye Louie gonna play clarinet with me and you and him oughta work good together. So I had taken the job and kept playing around at ELITE Cabaret, they call it. And they closed. And when they closed, they had another place open up there on Franklin, right over from 25, called it Lawler's Cabaret. Well, I got a job done. I worked right along. Up until the theater opened, I notified the fellow that I couldn't work any long because I promised John Robichaud I was going to work with him in the theater. So he wanted me to stay. He liked the way I played and everything. He wanted me to stay. Lee Collins had left here and went to Memphis. When he went to Memphis, he thought about Lee. He said, I can get you a good corner. He said, no, I want you. I said, how about Lee Collins? He says, oh yeah, that's right. Why could I reach Lee? I said, he's in Memphis. So somebody told him to address me. He wired Lee, you know. I gave him a two weeks notice, you know. Man, you're so glad to get Lee, you see. You know Lee could play that kind of music, you know. So he sent for Lee. And I had two weeks coming. He didn't pay no attention to that. He said, well, you can leave Wednesday coming. He said, he doesn't come back now, you know. I heard Lee was in town, you know. So to let him go to work too, I just told him I wasn't coming back no more. I went home and Lee took the job. He stayed there for a while. Then Lee went away. And Kid Punch took the job. Him and George, your boy, and they had a swinging little old band around there, you know. That stuff like to play around there, you know. And he took the job. Well, I got a job in other places then, you know. Left there. I had left and Lee took the job and then Poins taken. Let me see what I done. Then I had a job with Big Eye and Louis before the theater opened up, you know. And the next following week, me and Louis went to work together. No, we went together before when I went back. Piku was on that job. He was playing the alto strikes and playing there. Where did you work with them? So the union, the union, they got up a union and Piku didn't want to get in there, you see. And so they sent and got Louis anyway. Then me and Louis was working together. We had a girl playing piano. She was a very good musician. They called me. I told them about her, you know, and they placed her in the place of Miss Margaret. She's a great piano player too.
